source_text: Si \'deus\' commune uocabulum factum est uitio erroris humani, quatenus plures dei dicuntur atque creduntur in saeculo, benedictus tamen deus domini nostri Iesu Christi non alius quam creator intellegetur, qui et uniuersa benedixit — habes Genesim — et ab uniuersis benedicitur — habes Danihelem —; proinde si \'pater* potest dici sterilis deus, [nullius magis nomine quam creatoris] misericordiarum tamen pater idem erit, qui misericors et miserator et misericordiae plurimus dictus est. habes apud Ionam cum ipso misericordiae exemplum, quam Niniuitis exorantibus praestitit, facilis et Ezechiae fletibus flecti, et Achab, marito Iezabel, deprecanti sanguinem ignoscere Nabuthae, et Dauid agnoscenti delictum statim indulgens, malens scilicet paenitentiam peccatoris quam mortem, utique ex misericordiae adfectu. si quid tale Marcionis deus edidit uel edixit, agnoscam \'patrem misericordiarum\'. si uero ex eo tempore hunc titulum ei adscribit, quo reuelatus, quasi exinde sit (pater misericordiarum), quo liberare instituit genus humanum, atquin nos et ex eo tempore negamus illum, ex quo dicitur reuelatus. si enim prius constaret eum esse, tunc et adscribi ei posset. accidens enim est quod adscribitur, accidentia autem antecedit ipsius rei ostensio, cui accidunt. non potest igitur aliquid ei adscribere, quem tunc ostendit, cum aliquid ei adscribit; maxime cum iam alterius est quod adscribitur ei, qui prius non sit . ostensus. tanto (enim) magis negabitur esse, quanto per quod adfirmatur esse, eius est, qui iam ostensus est. Sic et \'testamentum nouum\' non alterius erit quam qui illud repromisit, etsi non litterae at eius spiritus - hoc erit nouitas-, (is) denique, qui litteram tabulis lapideis inciderat, idem et de spiritu edixerat: effundam de meo spiritu in omnem carnem; et si litter a occidit, spiritus uero uiuificat, eius utrumque est, qui ait: ego occidam et ego uiuificabo, percutiam et sanabo. olim duplicem uim creatoris uindicauimus. et iudicis et boni, littera occidentis per legem et spiritu uiuificantis per euangelium.
pass_a_gloss: If 'god' has become a common term due to the fault of human error, to the extent that many gods are said and believed in the world, nevertheless the blessed God of our Lord Jesus Christ is understood to be not other than the creator, who both blessed all things — you have Genesis — and is blessed by all things — you have Daniel —; therefore, if the 'father' can be said to be a sterile god, [with no one's name more than the creator's], nevertheless the same one will be the father of mercies, who is said to be merciful and a mercifier and most full of mercies. You have with Jonah himself an example of mercy, which he showed to the praying Ninevites, easily moved by the tears of Hezekiah, and to Ahab, the husband of Jezebel, forgiving the blood of Naboth when he prayed, and to David, immediately forgiving when he acknowledged his fault, certainly preferring the repentance of the sinner to death, from the affection of mercy. If Marcion's god has produced or decreed something of this kind, I will acknowledge 'the father of mercies'. But if he ascribes this title to him from that time when he was revealed, as if he were from then (the father of mercies), because he undertook to free the human race, then we deny him from that time when he is said to be revealed. For if it were previously established that he exists, then it could be ascribed to him. For what is ascribed is an accident, and accidents precede the showing of the thing to which they happen, to which they are ascribed. Therefore, nothing can be ascribed to him, whom he then shows, when he ascribes something to him; especially since what is ascribed to him already belongs to another, who was previously shown. He will be denied all the more to exist, insofar as what affirms him to exist is his, who has already been shown. Thus also 'the new testament' will not be of another than he who promised it, although not of the letter but of the spirit - this will be the newness -, (he) finally, who had inscribed the letter on stone tablets, also decreed concerning the spirit: I will pour out my spirit on all flesh; and if the letter kills, the spirit truly gives life, both are his, who says: I will kill and I will give life, I will strike and I will heal. Formerly we vindicated the double power of the creator, both of the judge and of the good, the letter killing through the law and the spirit giving life through the gospel.
pass_b_english: Because 'god' has become a common noun through the fault of human error — to the extent that many gods are named and believed in the world — the blessed God of our Lord Jesus Christ is understood to be none other than the Creator, who both blessed all things (you have Genesis) and is blessed by all things (you have Daniel). So if 'father' can be said of a sterile god [with no one's name more than the Creator's], the Father of Mercies will still be that same One who is called merciful, a mercifier, and most full of mercies. You have in Jonah an example of that mercy, which he showed to the praying Ninevites, easily moved by Hezekiah's tears, and to Ahab, Jezebel's husband, forgiving Naboth's blood when he pleaded, and to David, immediately pardoning him when he acknowledged his sin — preferring the sinner's repentance to death, precisely from the affection of mercy. If Marcion's god has ever produced or decreed anything of this kind, I will acknowledge 'the Father of Mercies.' But if he ascribes this title to him from the time he was revealed, as if he were from then on the Father of Mercies because he undertook to free the human race, then we deny him from that very time he is said to be revealed. For if it were previously established that he exists, then the title could be ascribed to him. An ascription is an accident, and accidents precede the showing of the thing to which they happen. Therefore nothing can be ascribed to him whom he then shows when he ascribes something to him; especially since what is ascribed to him already belongs to another who was previously shown. He will be denied all the more to exist, precisely because what affirms his existence belongs to the One who has already been shown. Thus also 'the new testament' will not belong to another than the One who promised it, although not of the letter but of the Spirit — that will be the newness — the same One who had inscribed the letter on stone tablets also decreed concerning the Spirit: I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and if the letter kills, the Spirit gives life — both are his, who says: I kill and I make alive, I wound and I heal. We have already vindicated the Creator's double power: both judge and good, the letter killing through the law and the Spirit giving life through the gospel.
